newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Protestant guerrillas say their truce holds.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Protestant guerrillas say their truce holds.

text.p: A key Protestant leader on Saturday denied pro-British guerrilla groups were behind the overnight murder of a Catholic in Belfast but did not rule out involvement by maverick gunmen.

David Ervine, a political ally of one of four banned extremist groups in the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), expressed "sadness and serious disappointment" over the killing, which fuelled fears of fresh sectarian violence.

Sinn Fein, the political wing of the outlawed Irish Republican Army (IRA), the Unionists' bitter enemy in conflict over British rule, blamed Unionist guerrillas and said the murder was evidence that shaky 29-month Unionist ceasefire had ended.
"I am as much in the dark as anyone in terms of who has actually caused the murder of this gentleman last evening," Ervine told reporters.
"However on numerous phone calls that I have made throughout the night and this morning I am fairly convinced that the Combined Loyalist Military Command are not responsible."
But he said it was possible maverick Loyalists might have shot 44-year-old John Slane, a father of nine, in his west Belfast home.
"That's a possiblity, I think we have got to wait and see. It certainly is a possibility and that must cause consternation to us all," he said.
A gunman burst into Slane's kitchen in Catholic nationalist West Belfast, and shot him as he prepared night-time hot milk bottles for his year-old twins, neighbours said.

Protestant guerrilla groups which support British rule have observed a truce since October 1994, six weeks after the IRA announced a ceasefire that lasted only until February 1996, when they unleashed a bombing wave on the British mainland.
But the Loyalist ceasefire has become increasingly unstable as IRA fighters step up their campaign of violence.

Loyalists are thought to have been behind a failed bomb attack on Sinn Fein premises in Monaghan town, in the Irish Republic, two weeks ago as a reprisal for the IRA's killing of a British soldier in Northern Ireland last month.

Ervine, a leader of the Progressive Unionist Party, was speaking at Belfast International Airport before he and politicians in the Ulster Democratic Party (UDP), which is also linked to banned guerrillas, left for a visit to Washington.

His calls for a redoubling of efforts to find a peaceful way out of the conflict was echoed by UDP leader Gary McMichael, who urged restraint from both Northern Ireland's pro-British Protestant majority and pro-Irish Catholic minority.
"If the Loyalist ceasefire were to end, then God help us all," he said.
Police said Slane was a guerrilla victim but refused to speculate on which shadowy underground group pulled the trigger.
Sinn Fein urged Catholics to be on alert. "This brutal murder was almost certainly the responsibility of a Loyalist death squad," it said in a statement
